column4: The section reads 95:4's خَلَقْنَا / تَقْوِيم as a maker measuring and straightening a human; this verse names the sequence خلق، فسوى، فعدل, so the artisan's careful proportion becomes explicit.
After fashioning and balancing the human, this ayah says God composed him in whatever صورة He willed; it completes the section's image of careful work reaching a finished form.

The section's root خ ل ق is glossed through measuring material before cutting, and أَحْسَن as working something well; here God “أَحْسَنَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقَهُ”, directly joining making and workmanship.
This continues the making process with “سَوَّاهُ” and the spirit, then gives hearing, sight and hearts; it shows the formed human as a deliberately furnished work.
This ayah says God created the heavens and earth in truth, then “صَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ”; its explicit good-forming closely matches the section's crafted human.
Alongside earth made as a dwelling and sky as a structure, the ayah says God formed and beautified human forms; it extends the section's workmanship image to the ordered world around the human.
The ayah says God created and formed humankind before commanding the angels to bow to Adam; it connects the section's well-made human to the dignity and response attached to that making.
God announces a human to be created from sounding clay; this gives the section's artisan image a specific raw material and staged act of making.
After the clay is formed, God says “نَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِنْ رُوحِي”; this marks the completion of the crafted body with a further divine act.
The human's beginning is traced to an extract of clay, supplying the material stage for the section's image of measured material being worked.
The extract becomes a drop placed in a secure resting place; this gives the human-making image an ordered intermediate stage.
The ayah traces successive formation through clot, lump, bones and flesh, then says “أَنشَأْنَاهُ خَلْقًا آخَرَ”; its closing “أَحْسَنُ الْخَالِقِينَ” makes the workman's quality explicit.
The human is recalled as a drop of emitted fluid; this starts another Qur'anic account of material shaped into a person.
The drop becomes a clinging substance and is then created and proportioned; the ayah gives the section's measured-making image a concrete sequence.
After creation and proportioning, the ayah distinguishes the two sexes; it presents differentiation as part of the finished form.
The rebuke “قُتِلَ الْإِنسَانُ” introduces a human who forgets the maker; its next ayat ask what he was made from, making the section's craftsmanship a ground for accountability.
The question “مِنْ أَيِّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقَهُ” directly names creation, the root whose dictionary sense the section develops as measuring material before cutting.
God's answer says He created the human and “فَقَدَّرَهُ”; the explicit apportioning gives the section's measurement-before-making detail a direct Qur'anic counterpart.
God creates people in their mothers' wombs “خَلْقًا مِنْ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ”; the ayah makes the section's crafted form a staged, hidden process.
“خَلَقَ فَسَوَّى” directly joins creation to proportioning, the same careful forming that the section hears in 95:4.
“قَدَّرَ فَهَدَى” joins measured allotment to guidance; it makes the section's claim that making begins with right measure visible in another concise formulation.
The ayah says God created every thing “بِقَدَرٍ”; this directly parallels the section's dictionary gloss of خَلْق as straight, measured apportionment.
After saying God created all things, the ayah says “فَقَدَّرَهُ تَقْدِيرًا”; creation and precise measure appear together, as in the section's account of measuring a hide before cutting.
While describing formation from dust through the womb, this ayah also names return to “أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ”; it supplies a bodily reading of the section's descent from the human's best form.
God creates people, then some are “يُرَدُّ إِلَىٰ أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ”; this is a direct bodily reversal for 95:5's return downward, without requiring the section's other, rejected-work sense of رَدّ.
The sequence weakness, strength, then weakness again makes bodily decline a concrete reversal of the section's image of a human made in the best proportion.
The ayah says that one granted long life is “نُنَكِّسْهُ فِي الْخَلْقِ”; this directly pictures a reversal within the created form, one possible bodily counterpart to 95:5.
The ayah follows human formation from dust and drop through maturity to old age and death; that life course clarifies how a carefully made form can decline.
Shuʿayb commands full measure and weight and forbids فساد on earth; this puts measured work and soundness opposite corruption, the same relation the section draws from خَلْق and صَلَح.
“أَوْفُوا الْكَيْلَ” and “زِنُوا بِالْقِسْطَاسِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ” give the section's measuring and straightening a concrete ethical scene of exact measure.
“أَوْفُوا الْكَيْلَ” begins a passage on full measure; it directly echoes the section's hide measured before cutting and frames craft as work that must be sound.
“وَزِنُوا بِالْقِسْطَاسِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ” supplies a straight balance, joining the section's straight spear and proper measurement in one image.
The warning not to deprive people of their things or spread فساد completes the measured-work passage by showing what a defective, corrupt practice does to others.

In the detailed debt-writing passage, God calls written terms “أَقْسَطُ” and “أَقْوَمُ لِلشَّهَادَةِ” and nearer to removing doubt; it joins measured craft, uprightness and the section's claim that a sound work admits no suspicion.
God raised the sky and set the “مِيزَان”; the image extends the section's measured making from human craft to an order established by God.
The command not to transgress the balance makes measured proportion a boundary against excess, complementing the section's straight measure.
The command to establish weight in justice and not make the balance deficient states the opposite of flawed measure in the section's craftsmanship image.

The torrent flows “بِقَدَرِهَا,” while foam rises from it and from metal heated for ornaments or tools; the foam vanishes but what benefits people remains. This unusually close meeting of measure, worked material, rejected byproduct and lasting useful work illuminates the section's crafted object and sound work.
The section explicitly cites “كِتَابٌ أُحْكِمَتْ آيَاتُهُ”; this ayah's firming then detailing of the verses is the Qur'anic example of ح ك م as work made secure.
After Satan's interference, God “يُحْكِمُ اللَّهُ آيَاتِهِ”; this directly develops the section's ح ك م branch as making something firm against corruption.

The distinction between “آيَاتٌ مُّحْكَمَاتٌ” and ambiguous verses gives context to the section's dictionary claim that the muhkam admits no suspicion; the ayah preserves the distinction rather than equating every verse with that quality.
The revealed book has no “عِوَجًا,” crookedness; this is a direct textual opposite to the section's straightening of a spear and its account of defective work.
The next ayah calls the book “قَيِّمًا”; it completes the prior claim of no crookedness with an upright, sound form, echoing the section's ق و م image.
The oath names the soul and “مَا سَوَّاهَا”; the same act of proportioning that makes the section's crafted human now frames the soul's moral possibilities.
The soul is shown its wickedness and its piety; this explains the choice that follows a well-proportioned human form in the section's account.
“قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّاهَا” gives the soul's successful refinement; it concretizes the section's صَلَح branch as soundness rather than فساد.
“وَقَدْ خَابَ مَن دَسَّاهَا” supplies the contrary outcome to refinement, matching the section's contrast between sound work and corruption.
The command not to spread فساد “بَعْدَ إِصْلَاحِهَا” directly joins corruption to the opposite of repair, the root relation the section draws for صَلَح.

In the contest with Moses, God declares that He does not set right the work of corrupters (“لَا يُصْلِحُ عَمَلَ الْمُفْسِدِينَ”); this directly joins عمل, إصلاح and فساد, the section's account of sound versus spoiled work.
The next ayah says God establishes truth by His words even when criminals dislike it; it completes the contest in 10:81 and clarifies the fate of corrupted work against what God makes firm.
People say “إِنَّمَا نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ” when told not to spread فساد; their claim of repair gives a specific counterexample to the section's sound-work sense of صَلَح.
The reply names them as corrupters while they do not perceive it; it completes 2:11 by separating claimed repair from actual soundness.
The objector asks who will give life to “الْعِظَامَ وَهِيَ رَمِيمٌ”; the broken, decayed bone recalls the section's dictionary branch for أَجْر as a fracture joining while the bone remains crooked.
The answer points to the One who produced the bones the first time; it ties the section's crafted creation to the possibility of restoring what has broken down.
The question about gathering “عِظَامَهُ” directly brings bones into the resurrection discussion, echoing the section's bone-fracture dictionary image.
God answers that He can proportion even the fingertips (“بَنَانَهُ”); this makes restoration a matter of exact forming, like the section's careful straightening and finishing.
The deniers ask whether they will be raised as bones and dust; the ayah makes the return of a finished body the issue.
The answer challenges them to imagine becoming stone or iron; it sharpens the material problem of a maker restoring what has dispersed.
The answer is the One who created them the first time; this closes the making-and-return sequence that surrounds the section's human craftsmanship.
God begins creation and repeats it, and the repetition is easier for Him; this directly links original making to restoration after decline.
God tests which people are “أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا”; the section's gloss of أَحْسَن as working a thing well helps connect crafted form to the quality of one's deeds.
Believers who do صالحات are promised “أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ”; this directly joins the section's sound works to its unending reward.
The same promise, “أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ,” follows faith and صالحات here; it is a close parallel to the section's finished-work and lasting-wage claim.
The ayah contrasts passing wealth and children with “الْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ,” which are better in reward and hope; it states what endures from good work against what passes.
After the creation and composition in 82:7–8, this ayah says people deny the Recompense; it completes the parallel to 95:4–7, where the made human is challenged about judgment.
God calls His way “صِرَاطِي مُسْتَقِيمًا” and contrasts it with other paths; the section's straightened spear gives a physical counterpart to this straight course and its deviations.
The Qur'an guides to “لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ”; this carries the section's ق و م straightness from crafted object into a rightly directed way.
God's way is “قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ,” while other ways deviate; this gives the section's straight-course image a concrete contrast with crooked direction.
The ayah describes whoever wills to take “سَبِيلًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا”; it offers the same straight-course image that the section develops through the spear shaft.
The command “فَاسْتَقِمْ كَمَا أُمِرْتَ” turns straightness into a commanded stance; it connects the section's physical straightening to faithful conduct.
Those who say their Lord is God and then “اسْتَقَامُوا” receive the promise of no fear; the section's straightness becomes a sustained human response to the maker.
This repeats “اسْتَقَامُوا” for those who affirm God and promises no fear or grief; it extends the section's straight-course image to steady conduct and its result.

The promise of abundant water is attached to people who “اسْتَقَامُوا عَلَى الطَّرِيقَةِ”; this gives a concrete consequence to the straightness motif, though the passage concerns a community's conduct rather than craft.

This neighbor of the foam-and-metal parable distinguishes those who answer their Lord from those who do not and names their opposed outcomes; it completes 13:17's useful remainder/vanishing foam with a judgment contrast.
The Prophet is told he has “لَأَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ”; here the section's uncut-wage phrase applies to the Prophet's labor, rather than specifically to believers' صالحات.
The command to be patient is followed by the claim that God does not waste the reward of good-doers; it states the endurance of worthwhile work that the section's reward image implies.
God says He does not allow any worker's work to be lost; this directly supports the section's contrast between rejected spoiled work and the lasting wage for sound deeds.

The forbidden “الْأَزْلَامِ” are arrows used to seek a decision; they give the section's carefully straightened arrow a contrary use as a lot, though the Qur'anic arrows are divining arrows rather than a craftsman's tool.
The sky is made in layers with no “تَفَاوُتٍ”; this reverses the section's dictionary example of a face whose defect turns the gaze away, presenting creation as free of mismatch.

The repeated gaze returns humbled after finding no flaw; the section's ر د د dictionary wording says ugliness can “يَرُدُّ الطَّرْفَ,” so this is a specific reversal in which the eye returns because the work is flawless.
The deeds of those who reject their Lord are compared to ashes scattered by wind; this gives a concrete image for work that cannot remain, opposite the section's sound work and lasting wage.
Those who deny God's signs and meeting Him have deeds made fruitless; it parallels the section's rejected defective product, with the cause specified by this ayah's own context.
Hypocrites are assigned “الدَّرْكِ الْأَسْفَلِ” of the Fire; if 95:5's low return is read as final moral descent, this supplies a specific lowest-depth counterpart.
The record of the wicked is placed in “سِجِّينٍ”; if the section's “أَسْفَلَ سَافِلِينَ” points to final spiritual lowliness, this gives that descent a record and judgment setting.
The record of the righteous is placed in “عِلِّيِّينَ,” a high counter-image to the section's low return and its exception for believers' sound works.

After created proportion and measure, the pasture is made into dark stubble; this is a concrete created thing losing its flourishing form, a limited parallel to the section's best-made human being brought low.
The arrow used for divination is a boundary against the section's measured, corrected arrow: a crafted instrument is turned to chance-seeking rather than skilled work.
